# Charcoal burning (`charcoal_burning`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Core idea: Wood heated with almost no air does not burn but chars: the water and tarry vapours are driven off and a carbon-rich solid containing ash and residual volatile material is left. Stack dry billets tightly around a central flue, cover the heap with turf and earth, light it down the flue and control the draught through a few holes at the base for several days, closing every hole where flame shows, until the smoke turns from white to thin blue; then seal it completely and let it cool. Five to seven tonnes of wood give one tonne of charcoal; a well-managed mound can yield about 20–25 % of the dry wood mass. Charcoal burns hotter and cleaner than wood, with little sulphur. It supplied both heat and a reducing atmosphere in many furnaces before the adoption of coke. Coppiced woodland cut on a 15 to 20 year cycle supplies it for ever; clear felling does not.
- Pitfalls:
  - Letting in too much air, so the heap burns to ash; or opening it while hot, when it catches fire; a mound can also collapse
  - Walking on the heap: burners fell through the crust into the fire
  - Burning charcoal in a closed room; the fumes (carbon monoxide) kill without smell
  - Thinking raw coal can simply replace charcoal in ironmaking; its sulphur ruins the iron
  - Underestimating the wood needed: a tonne of iron took the charcoal from several tonnes of wood, so forests set the limit
  - Wet or freshly quenched charcoal; stored damp or in big warm heaps it can also ignite by itself
- History: mesopotamia: 5th–4th millennium BC – charcoal fuels the first copper smelting in the Near East and Iran; egypt: 3rd millennium BC – charcoal for metalworking shown in tomb scenes; china: 2nd millennium BC – charcoal for bronze casting; from the Han, coal partly replaces it, in iron by the 11th c. AD; africa: 1st millennium BC – charcoal iron smelting in West, Central and East Africa; americas: 1st millennium BC – charcoal for Andean copper and gold working; europe: antiquity onward; mound burning described by Theophrastus (c. 300 BC) and in detail by Biringuccio (1540); wood shortage drives the 18th c. shift to coke in Britain; global: charcoal accompanies early copper smelting from c. 5000 BC; older still as a pigment and fuel
- Read:
  - Theophrastus, Enquiry into Plants V.9
  - Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540; tr. C. S. Smith & M. T. Gnudi, 1942)
  - Vaclav Smil, Energy and Civilization: A History (2017)
  - Lewis Dartnell, The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World from Scratch (2014)
